author: Madolin Edwards
title: Early steam engines, tractors and horse power highlight 74th Jubilee - NewsBreak
text:
By Madolin Edwards ,
19 hours ago Do you know how to thresh? What about flail?
A trip to the 74th Farmers and Threshermen's Jubilee Sept. 9-13 will teach you how to do both, make apple cider and so much more.
The Jubilee, held at 3054 Kingwood Road in New Centerville, showcases the early machines of agricultural life, from steam engines and early gasoline tractors to horse- and dog-powered machines. It is sponsored by and benefits the New Centerville and Rural Volunteer Fire Co.
During the Jubilee, visitors can see demonstrations of a steam-powered cider mill, ground hog thresher flailers, horse power with tumbling shaft machine, first steam engine threshing with hand feeding, self-feeder threshing, baling up straw, blacksmith, stone crusher, dog-powered butter churning, flour mill, antique power saws, steam-powered sawmill and shingle making, corn shelling, corn shredding, blacksmithing, feed grinder machine, handle machine, broom making, a 75 horsepower Fairbanks Morris engine, a 150 horse-powered Reeves propane gas engine, an 800 horse-powered Chicago pneumatic diesel engine, antique tractors, hit-and-miss gas engines and steam-engine plowing.
The Jubilee volunteers demonstrate threshing from its beginning, using horse-powered threshing and then a steam-powered threshing machine. Early farmers shelled small amounts of grain by hand or beat harvested sheaves against the ground or with a stick, according to Michele Beener, a representative of the Jubilee committee. The manual grain flail, a short wooden stick tied to a longer handle with a leather strap or cord, became a standard tool in the 18th century.
For treading, loosened sheaves is spread over circular stone or flattened earth enclosures and livestock like oxen or sheep are driven over them to crush the husks, Beener said. After threshing, farmers tossed the mixture into the air for winnowing – the wind blows away the lightweight chaff while the heavy grain falls back down.
Combines handle all this today.
"My grandfather, MJ Miller, who was a Jubilee volunteer from the first show until 1991 when he passed, farmed in Middlecreek," said Beener. "My dad, Michael J. Miller, has been at every Jubilee except one for basic training, and has restored many of the items you’ll see on the grounds which the family owns and operates today."
What goes on at the Jubilee? There are demonstrations and other activities each day. Gates open at 10 a.m. Plenty of parking is available in the field.
There will be 15 big steam tractors on display. Steam engine games and plowing will be held. Registrations are on Sept. 8 in the banquet hall and Museum Hall for quilts, photos, scarecrow contest and pumpkin-decorating contest entries. Registration for Grandma Hazel's Apple Pie Contest is Wednesday, Sept. 8. The winning pies will be sold at 8:15 p.m.
The 2026 Jubilee quilt design is Birthday Tulips and is queen sized (88 x 108). It was sewn and quilted by Rosemarie Younkin, Markleton. The steam engine cross-stitched patch was made by Sue Miller. Quilts should be registered between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. Tuesday, Sept. 7, for the show. A 2 p.m. Sept. 13 auction will be held.
Other specialty contests include the longest beard and corn hole tournament. The Steam Ahead 5K Walk and Run is on Sept. 12, along with horseshoe pitching contest, chicken barbecue and Tractor Buddies Tractor Square Dancing and a tug of war with steam engines. A steam engine spark show is featured each evening.
"We have our steam engines spark show which is the country-form of fireworks. It's a favorite of the visitors," Beener said. "The steam engine plowing, weather permitting, people love to take photos of. It's therapeutic, watching the steam engine plowing in the field."
There will be a craft show and flea market in the craft building which opens at 10 a.m. each day. Entertainment in the main building is constant. At 1 p.m. a parade of tractors will be a little longer this year, Beener said. Kids day activities on Sept. 12 includes a pedal power tractor pull for ages 3-6, and hay bale toss for ages 7-12. Call Kaitlyn Miller at 814-442-8365 to register. Dave Weyant has a 1/2 size tractor that he gets as many children as possible to play in a tug of war with him at 3 p.m. Thursday, Sept. 10, Michael Miller, also a member of the Jubilee committee, said.
There will be model and display hit-and-miss engines. Rockwood Historical Society will have a booth to do genealogy.
"They have experts on all the graveyards in the county. Clark Brocht is quite an expert on the graveyards. People from far away are interested in finding family members," Beener said.
Tractor and truck pulls by Appalachian Outlaws will be held. An ATV pull is 6:30 p.m. Sept. 10, garden tractor pull is at 6:30 p.m. and dead weight pull is at 6:30 p.m. Sept. 11 is the farm tractor pull at 6:30. and Sept. 12 the pull begins at 7 p.m. Sept. 13 is the semi and 4X4 pick up pull at 12 p.m.
Sept. 9 is community day and free admission. The Grand Jubilee Parade is at 6:15 p.m. A crew from the USS Somerset will be in the parade, Beener said.
"It's as big as always and goes until dark," Beener said. "The event gets bigger and bigger every year."
The Jubilee Queen Contest at 7:45 p.m. The Outhouse Dash, a privy on wheels race, will launch at 8:15 p.m. The Jubilee Queen and King will be crowned at 8:30 p.m. in the Museum Hall.
Wood carving demonstrations are Sept. 9-12 with the auction at 5:30 p.m. Sept. 12. Miller said the blacksmith shop will make special requested items right there for visitors.
"Have a seat and you can watch them and rest," said Beener. "The cider mill and flour and cornmeal mill will be running. Oliver tractor is the feature this year."
Beener said the best breakfast you'll ever have is served from 7-9 a.m. A chicken barbecue will be held from 11 a.m. Sept. 12 and 13. Sept. 13 events start with a community church service.
"We have things going on all the time," Miller said. "There is no limit to the activities."
Behind the scenes work Miller said visitors have no idea about all the work that goes on behind the scenes to make sure the Jubilee is ready to go each year.
Apple cider is made with a steam boiler and generator running the large commercial size press. With the shortage of fresh apples in the tri-state area, the cost for apples has more than doubled this year. An orchard from the Wexford area will take a 53-foot refrigerated trailer east to various orchards and pick up enough apples to fill the 1,000-bushel order.
"There are no apples locally, so we had to go to New York to get 1,000 bushels of apples for the mill," Miller and Beener said. "That's why the price of the apple products is going to be a little higher this year."
They also have boiler inspections that take several days to make sure the owners follow federal and state rules for boilers, Miller said. The committee has also relighted the grounds with new lights.
QR code for pieces Small Town Steam, a local community effort to categorize the history of the steam and vintage agricultural equipment locally and across the country, is putting QR codes in place to explain the different machines, Miller said. The QR codes are educational. Visitors are recommended to bring a smart phone. Miller said people will be posted at different times during the day to explain activities and displays.
"The Small Town Steam ladies are doing a good job of documenting the Jubilee," Miller said.
Beener said next year is the Jubilee’s 75th Diamond Anniversary and the organizers are looking for early Jubilee photos. Miller and Beener asked visitors who may have photos or stories to tell to stop at the information booth, or email Michele at mrmbeener@gmail.com . She is looking for old photos from the early years of the Farmers and Threshermen's Jubilee and people who have attended all 75 years.
This article originally appeared on The Daily American: Early steam engines, tractors and horse power highlight 74th Jubilee
